domain: Comparative Law / Political Theory / Religious Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of India's parallel personal-law system where Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi, and secular legal frameworks govern marriage and family matters simultaneously within one state. The system has persisted for decades without zero-sum displacement, raising the question of whether this represents one contested kernel (marriage/family authority) read through multiple traditions, or fundamentally incoherent bundles of distinct kernels that happen to coexist.

key_entities: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 (codified Hindu personal law)
Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 (Islamic jurisprudence framework)
Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872 (Christian denominational law)
Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936 (Zoroastrian community law)
Special Marriage Act 1954 (secular civil marriage option)
Indian Supreme Court (constitutional adjudicator; UCC debate arbiter)
All India Muslim Personal Law Board (interpretive authority for Muslim law)
key_tensions: Community autonomy vs uniform citizenship (personal law preservation vs Uniform Civil Code)
Religious authority vs state sovereignty (who interprets marriage validity)
Gender equality vs traditional practice (Shah Bano case; triple talaq reform)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Authority to define valid marriage, divorce, inheritance, and custody — the boundary of legitimate family formation and dissolution
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Contested across five parallel systems: religious texts/clergy (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi) vs secular state legislature

readings.commitment: Marriage as sacramental samskara governed by dharmic texts and customary practice
readings.authority_grounding: Vedic/Puranic scripture interpreted through regional custom; codified 1955-56 Acts as state compromise
readings.expected_structural_delta: Sacramental indissolubility (pre-1955); caste endogamy norms; joint family property rules; wife as ritual participant not autonomous contractor

readings.commitment: Marriage as civil contract (nikah) governed by Quranic injunctions and hadith
readings.authority_grounding: Shariat courts and ulama interpretation; 1937 Act preserves pre-colonial Islamic jurisprudence
readings.expected_structural_delta: Contractual dissolution (talaq); polygyny permitted; mahr (dower) obligation; gender-asymmetric divorce access (pre-2019 triple talaq ban)

readings.commitment: Marriage as sacrament under ecclesiastical authority (Catholic) or denominational governance (Protestant)
readings.authority_grounding: Canon law (Catholic) or denominational synods; 1872 Act codifies Christian practice
readings.expected_structural_delta: Sacramental permanence (Catholic no-divorce); denominational variance (Protestant divorce permitted); church authority over validity

readings.commitment: Marriage as community-preserving institution governed by Zoroastrian religious law
readings.authority_grounding: Parsi panchayats and Zoroastrian clergy; 1936 Act codifies community practice
readings.expected_structural_delta: Endogamy requirement (loss of community status for intermarriage); priestly authority over ritual validity; small-community preservation logic

readings.commitment: Marriage as civil contract between autonomous individuals under state law
readings.authority_grounding: Parliamentary legislation (Special Marriage Act 1954); Supreme Court constitutional review
readings.expected_structural_delta: No religious requirement; gender-symmetric rights; state registration as sole validity criterion; interfaith marriage permitted

axiom_contradictions.basis: Sacramental ontology (marriage as cosmic/ritual bond transcending individual will) cannot coexist with contractual ontology (marriage as revocable agreement between autonomous parties) in a single coherent framework
Contractual dissolution as divinely permitted (Quranic talaq) contradicts sacramental indissolubility (Catholic permanence) — no framework holds both as simultaneously valid
Ecclesiastical authority as necessary for validity (sacrament requires church) contradicts state-only authority (civil registration sufficient) — mutually exclusive sovereignty claims
Community-boundary preservation (endogamy as religious duty) contradicts individual autonomy (interfaith marriage as protected right) — incompatible conceptions of legitimate choice

axes.structural_delta: Five mutually exclusive readings of what grounds legitimate marriage/divorce authority coexist without resolution

axes.selection_reason: Core kernel with five distinct readings; highest centrality; upstream to all other axes

omegas.description: Is this genuinely one kernel read five ways, or five incoherent kernels bundled by colonial accident? The axiom contradictions suggest the latter, but the system's 70-year persistence without collapse suggests licensed plurality may stabilize incoherence.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel/reading decomposition; D2 culture-level break test

omegas.description: Special Marriage Act provides formal exit, but social costs (community ostracism, family pressure) create asymmetric exit barriers. Is this a Rope (coordination cost) or Snare (deliberate entrapment)?

Supreme Court interventions (Shah Bano reversal, triple talaq ban) suggest partial drift status, but unclear whether judiciary is absorbing drift or forcing kernel revision. May reclassify from licensed_plurality to contested_succession.

Would a Uniform Civil Code replace five kernels with one, or merely add a sixth reading? If the latter, the system's structure (licensed plurality) persists; if the former, it's a regime change not a reading addition.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition applied per §1.3-K. Five readings selected based on distinct authority_grounding and expected_structural_delta. Two ordinary axes (gender_asymmetry_extraction, constitutional_federalism_tension) pass §3 independence test. Deferred minority_rights_shield due to overlap with gender axis.
